items.name: Lang-SVG: Hierarchical Image Vectorization with Language Priors
items.repository: Lang-SVG: Hierarchical Image Vectorization with Language Priors
items.description: Image vectorization reconstructs raster images as compact scalable vector graph- ics (SVG), providing a structured and editable code representation of images. However, most existing vectorization methods optimize for pixel-level render- ing fidelity, often producing SVGs that lack alignment with human-perceived object-part hierarchies, making them difficult to manipulate. To address this, we propose Lang-SVG, which introduces an explicit tree structure to organize SVG primitives with semantic labels and parent-child relationships. Lang-SVG incorporates granularity-controllable and open-vocabulary segmentation priors to initialize object-part hierarchies and leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with SVG tree context to assign semantic labels to unlabeled nodes. To reduce redundancy, we introduce depth-adaptive simplification to reduce shape complexity and Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging to eliminate redundant SVG nodes. L1-SAM-Prompting further recovers missing regions to improve recon- struction fidelity and structural completeness. Beyond reconstruction fidelity, we introduce a new evaluation protocol that measures structural quality and semantic part alignment. Experiments demonstrate that Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art performance in both rendering fidelity and structural quality. Project website: https://xiliu8006.github.io/Lang-SVG/.

items.name: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
items.repository: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
items.description: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.

items.name: A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
items.repository: A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
items.description: Pretrained language models (LMs) remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters. We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-grafting primitives that compile deterministic computation directly into pretrained LM weights using zero training examples and zero runtime hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization drift and preserving natural-language (NL) competence. Our construction combines three analytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scaling into translation along a log-spaced gate grid (>250times dynamic range) with IEEE 754 error bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned width extension (d to d+K) with d/(d+K) norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE emission, and differential (+254,-256) tied unembeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4-8 digit signed {+,-,times} circuits in constant TC^0 depth alongside 3-literal Boolean (100%, N=1{,}728; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits. On 6-digit arithmetic (N=1{,}200, BF16), IBM Granite 4.2 3B (1.07M-1.33M active non-zeros, le 0.036%) and Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B (2.25M-2.39M non-zeros, le 0.057%) reach 99.17% and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with an FP32 sidecar) and 98%-100% mid-sentence resumption, outperforming 12.8K-sample LoRA (42.2% / 61.7%, 0% inline continuation). A factorized block-sparse sidecar holds A100 memory at 7.89 / 10.65 GiB (4.60 / 8.14 GiB under INT8/INT4 + FP32 sidecar) while passing all 14/14 pre-registered >2K-token Tango splits (N=4{,}392; 0/11,134 OOD triggers).

items.name: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
items.repository: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
items.description: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.

items.name: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
items.repository: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
items.description: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

items.name: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
items.repository: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
items.description: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp

items.name: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators
items.repository: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators
items.description: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.

items.name: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search
items.repository: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search
items.description: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with grep. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over 91 repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.

items.name: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
items.repository: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
items.description: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

items.name: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
items.repository: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
items.description: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

items.name: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning
items.repository: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning
items.description: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.

items.name: WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models
items.repository: WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models
items.description: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.

items.name: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
items.repository: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
items.description: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

items.name: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning
items.repository: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning
items.description: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.

items.name: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First
items.repository: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First
items.description: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.

items.name: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
items.repository: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
items.description: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

items.name: Choosing Quantized Code LLMs by File Size and Energy per Solved Task
items.repository: Choosing Quantized Code LLMs by File Size and Energy per Solved Task
items.description: A developer running a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. A common rule says a larger model at lower precision tends to beat a smaller one at higher precision. We ran 24 GGUF files of Qwen2.5-Coder at four sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 and priced each in energy per solved task on 542 EvalPlus tasks. The result is a selection guide indexed by Ollama's listed file size, with an evidence label on each pick. At 1 and 2 GB it picks the q4_K_M files of the 1.5B and 3B models, both on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B file that fits, and there it does not pay. That file brings no significant gain in solves over the 2 GB pick, 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deficit to 2.4 points. Yet 7B-q2_K needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task on CPU, GPU and memory rails, or 1.66 to 1.81 times on whole-system power. On HumanEval+, five alternating session pairs give a ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid. At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys a significant gain over the 2 GB pick at a higher energy price. From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI). We release per-task results, power logs and the analysis script.

items.name: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
items.repository: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
items.description: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.

items.name: PGPO: Prototype-Guided Progressive Obfuscation for Privacy-Preserving LLM-Enhanced Recommendation
items.repository: PGPO: Prototype-Guided Progressive Obfuscation for Privacy-Preserving LLM-Enhanced Recommendation
items.description: LLM-enhanced recommender systems encode item side information into semantic embeddings, but these embeddings may leak sensitive textual attributes through inversion attacks. Existing input-side defenses rely on trusted collection or local token perturbation, often disrupting the inter-item semantic topology needed for recommendation. To address it, we introduce relational fidelity as the key objective, requiring semantic shift for privacy while preserving relative item relations for utility. Based on this principle, we propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (PGPO), which learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words and propagates them through a static semantic graph. PGPO is optimized with GRPO using individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint rewards. Experiments on two benchmarks show strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation performance. The code is available at https://github.com/Shengxiang-Lin/PGPO.

items.name: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
items.repository: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
items.description: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

items.name: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
items.repository: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
items.description: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs (geq 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran 2.3times, 9.1times, and 40.9times faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.

items.name: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests
items.repository: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests
items.description: Experimentation teams must decide which proposed website changes to test with live traffic. We evaluated whether forecasts from simulated shoppers could inform that choice. We screened 412 historical website A/B tests and evaluated four systems on the 318 that ran longer than 21 days. Each system predicted an original win, a variant win, or an inconclusive result. Page roles were masked and recorded outcomes were withheld during inference. Squoosh UX-1, a model fine-tuned on human browsing data, simulated 1,000 shoppers per arm and correctly classified 267 of 318 outcomes (84.0%, 95% Wilson interval 79.5-87.6%, treating experiments as independent). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest general-purpose configuration on outcome accuracy, correctly classified 196 of 318 (61.6%). UX-1 favored the variant in 126 experiments. In the live tests, 118 of those variants won (93.7%), four lost, and four had inconclusive results. The remaining 192 experiments included 19 additional variant wins.

items.name: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.repository: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.description: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.

items.name: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models
items.repository: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models
items.description: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63times speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.

items.name: WAM-Policy: World Action Models with On-Policy Distillation for Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation
items.repository: WAM-Policy: World Action Models with On-Policy Distillation for Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation
items.description: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.

items.name: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts
items.repository: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts
items.description: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.

items.name: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
items.repository: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
items.description: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

items.name: BLIP-Live: Balancing Timeliness & Firing Precision in Proactive Streaming Video Agents
items.repository: BLIP-Live: Balancing Timeliness & Firing Precision in Proactive Streaming Video Agents
items.description: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.

items.name: WaveView: The Novel View Is in the Noise
items.repository: WaveView: The Novel View Is in the Noise
items.description: Generative novel view synthesis (NVS) employs a diffusion model to render a static or dynamic scene from a target camera view. Explicit warp methods complete a reprojection of the source with video diffusion models, and implicit methods encode the camera parameters or 3D cues. Both add inference overhead, and the generated layout often drifts from the ground truth. We present WaveView, which injects the warped source into the phase of the initial noise of a pretrained generator. The Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform (DT-CWPT) allows local and anisotropic phase injection. The generator is thus constrained less in disoccluded regions and along the epipolar line. WaveView keeps the architecture and adds negligible overhead. On the DL3DV benchmark, it outperforms all baselines in every overlap bin. In the hardest bin, it gains 0.84 dB PSNR on the covisible region over MetaView, which shares its generator, while running 2.1 times faster. For dynamic NVS, fine-tuning AnyView with the same noise raises its zero-shot PSNR on AnyViewBench from 11.58 to 12.35 dB.

items.name: AVTR: Adaptive Multimodal Reasoning with Visual Imagination
items.repository: AVTR: Adaptive Multimodal Reasoning with Visual Imagination
items.description: Vision-Language Models increasingly rely on textual reasoning to solve advanced multimodal tasks. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm faces two fundamental limitations. First, relying on textual reasoning alone can limit perceptual ability in vision-centric questions, where accurate answers depend on interpreting task-relevant visual evidence. Second, applying textual reasoning uniformly across inputs overlooks question-dependent variation in both reasoning modality and depth, often producing verbose and unnecessary traces when little logical inference is required. To this end, we propose Adaptive Visual-Textual Reasoning (AVTR), which introduces visual imagination as a complementary reasoning modality to textual thinking, enabling the model to revisit its visual observations and distill the salient evidence through generative visual reflection. Furthermore, we formulate reasoning-modality selection as a learned routing problem, allowing a single policy to adaptively harness the complementary strengths of visual reflection and textual reasoning in response to the perceptual and inferential demands of the input. Across 16 benchmarks, AVTR improves the average score by 4.5 points over Qwen3.5 baseline, while reducing inference latency by 33\%. It also scales effectively into a smaller size backbone, outperforming the evaluated 2B-scale baselines.

items.name: Out of Sight, Still in Mind: Token Compression for Omni-LLMs
items.repository: Out of Sight, Still in Mind: Token Compression for Omni-LLMs
items.description: The goal of this paper is to reduce the input token cost of Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) at inference time. Omni-LLMs reason jointly over audio, video and text, but the cost of the three streams is highly unbalanced: visual tokens account for the vast majority of the input, and are highly redundant. In this paper, we propose ReMo, a training-free framework that compresses visual tokens by redistributing their information across modalities: a visual token is kept only if its information appears nowhere else. ReMo achieves this in two ways: (i) it aligns audio and video in a shared space via closed-form calibration, and removes visual tokens already explained by the audio or by other visual tokens; and (ii) it replaces object-level visual tokens, identified by a lightweight object detector, with compact text proxies, short descriptions of each object and its location, conveying the same content in far fewer tokens. On Qwen2.5-Omni at two model scales, ReMo removes 54% of the input tokens with comparable accuracy. It performs comparably to the full-token model, reaching 101.2% and 101.4% of its average accuracy over five audio-visual benchmarks.

items.name: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
items.repository: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
items.description: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

items.name: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
items.repository: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
items.description: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

items.name: Tideway: Phase-Aware Tiered Memory Management for MoE Inference on Consumer Devices
items.repository: Tideway: Phase-Aware Tiered Memory Management for MoE Inference on Consumer Devices
items.description:
Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly becoming a dominant paradigm for AI applications. Recently, there is a growing demand to deploy large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models locally on consumer PCs to balance data privacy, API costs, and inference efficiency. However, unlike datacenter servers with abundant DRAM, consumer devices are tightly constrained in both GPU VRAM and host RAM, forcing massive MoE weights to spill across VRAM, host RAM, and SSD. Under such spilling, we observe that existing systems fail to fully utilize this memory hierarchy, treating the tiers as independent caches and thrashing in inference.
  We present TIDEWAY, a system for efficient inference of large MoE models on memory-constrained consumer devices. Our core insight is to manage host RAM and GPU VRAM as a unified memory pool. Within this pool, TIDEWAY couples phase-aware memory layouts, which adapt to the distinct access patterns of prefill and decode, with an execution engine that optimizes CUDA Graph execution under expert paging. Our evaluations on representative consumer hardware with frontier MoE models demonstrate that TIDEWAY significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems. On average, TIDEWAY achieves speedups of 1.97x in end-to-end latency and 2.40x in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), along with 1.61x higher decode throughput against the fastest baseline.
  Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/Tideway .

items.name: Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation
items.repository: Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation
items.description: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.

items.name: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models
items.repository: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models
items.description: Flow-based generative models are trained on a hand-chosen prediction target, such as the velocity, the noise, or the clean data. This choice strongly affects training and sample quality. We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces a fixed prediction target with a fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically, assigning a separate nonnegative weight to each direction in a jointly learned basis. A closed-form map recovers the velocity from the network's prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. Since recovery is exact, training optimizes the target purely to make it easier for the network to predict. We theoretically analyze the resulting prediction error and predict that the preferred noise weight in each direction scales near-linearly with data variance, in agreement with the weights learned empirically in pixel space. AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT baseline on ImageNet 256times256, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. In pixel-space text-to-image generation, AnisoFlow improves image quality and, through better-conditioned velocity recovery, largely removes patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference.

items.name: Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
items.repository: Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
items.description: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

items.name: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models
items.repository: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models
items.description: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.
